title: Python Concurrency Explained: Threading, Multiprocessing & Asyncio (Full Guide)
description:
Python gives you three different ways to run work concurrently, and each one solves a different problem. This video walks through the full picture: why the Global Interpreter Lock makes threading great for I/O but useless for CPU-heavy code, why multiprocessing is the real fix for CPU-bound work, how asyncio's single-threaded event loop handles thousands of I/O tasks without any threads at all, and how Python 3.11's structured concurrency -- TaskGroup, except*, and asyncio.timeout -- makes async code safe to run in production instead of silently losing failed tasks. Every code example is pulled directly from the Python Mastery Path curriculum, in the order covered below.

beats.narration: Python gives you three different ways to do many things at once, and picking the wrong one can make your code slower, not faster. In this video we'll walk through threading and multiprocessing for classic concurrency, then dive into asyncio's event loop, and finish with the structured concurrency patterns that make asyncio safe to use in real production code.

Let's start with the two oldest tools in Python's concurrency toolbox: threads and processes. The key to using either one well is understanding a single piece of CPython internals -- the Global Interpreter Lock.

CPython's Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, even on a machine with eight cores. So if you spin up four threads to crunch through a CPU-heavy loop like this one, you won't see much speedup at all -- they're all fighting over that same lock.

display.code:
import threading
import time

def cpu_bound(n):
    count = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        count += 1
    return count

start = time.perf_counter()
threads = [threading.Thread(target=cpu_bound, args=(20_000_000,)) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(f"threaded: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")   # not much faster than sequential

beats.narration: But the GIL gets released the moment a thread is waiting on something -- a network call, a disk read, or here, a simulated sleep. Fire off five of these simulated downloads on separate threads and they wait together, so the whole batch finishes in about one second instead of five.

Threads sharing state is where things get dangerous. Two threads incrementing the same counter can read and write at overlapping times and lose updates in between. Wrapping the increment in a lock, like this, forces one thread at a time through that critical section, so the final count comes out exactly right.

display.code:
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def increment(n):
    global counter
    for _ in range(n):
        with lock:      # only one thread can hold the lock at a time
            counter += 1


threads = [threading.Thread(target=increment, args=(100_000,)) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(counter)

beats.narration: For CPU-bound work, multiprocessing is the real fix. Each process gets its own interpreter and its own GIL, so a pool of four processes actually runs on four cores in parallel. Notice the if-name-equals-main guard -- it's required, because worker processes re-import your script and would otherwise try to spawn their own pools recursively.

display.code:
import multiprocessing
import time

def cpu_bound(n):
    count = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        count += 1
    return count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    start = time.perf_counter()
    with multiprocessing.Pool(processes=4) as pool:
        results = pool.map(cpu_bound, [20_000_000] * 4)
    print(f"multiprocessing: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")   # noticeably faster on multi-core machines

beats.narration: concurrent.futures gives threads and processes the same interface, so ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor are basically a one-line swap. Submit your I/O-bound fetches to a thread pool, collect results as they complete, and if the work turns CPU-bound later, you just change one class name.

executor.map is the simpler variant -- hand it a function and a list of inputs, and it gives back results in the exact order you submitted them, no manual bookkeeping of futures required. Reach for this when you just want all the results once everything's done.

display.code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def square(n):
    return n * n

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
    results = list(executor.map(square, range(10)))

print(results)

beats.narration: So how do you actually choose? If you're waiting on the network or disk, reach for threading -- the GIL releases during those waits, so overhead stays low. If you're crunching numbers, reach for multiprocessing -- it sidesteps the GIL entirely with separate processes. And whenever multiple threads touch the same mutable state, a lock is what keeps it from corrupting.

display.heading: Choosing the right tool
display.subheading: I/O-bound -> threading  |  CPU-bound -> multiprocessing  |  shared state -> a Lock

beats.narration: Threads and processes are powerful, but they come with real overhead -- context switches, memory copies, and the ever-present risk of race conditions. Next, let's see how asyncio gets I/O concurrency without needing any of that.

display.heading: From threads and processes to a single event loop
display.subheading: Next up: I/O concurrency without any threads at all

beats.narration: Asyncio flips the model entirely. Instead of the operating system switching between threads, you write coroutines with async def, and a single-threaded event loop decides when each one runs -- cooperatively, at every await point.

Calling an async function doesn't run it immediately -- it just creates a coroutine object. Await is what actually drives it forward, running it until it either finishes or hits its own await, like this asyncio.sleep, which yields control back to the event loop instead of blocking.

display.code:
import asyncio

async def say_after(delay, message):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)   # non-blocking sleep -- yields control to the event loop
    print(message)
    return message


async def main():
    result = await say_after(1, "hello")
    print(f"got: {result}")


asyncio.run(main())

beats.narration: Here's a trap beginners fall into: awaiting two tasks back to back, one at a time, gives you zero concurrency benefit. It's exactly as slow as calling them synchronously -- about two seconds for two one-second sleeps, because nothing else gets a chance to run in between.

display.code:
import asyncio
import time

async def task(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    print(f"{name} done")


async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    await task("A", 1)
    await task("B", 1)
    print(f"sequential: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")   # ~2s -- one after another


asyncio.run(main())

beats.narration: asyncio.gather is what actually runs coroutines together. While one task is parked inside a sleep, the event loop hands control to the others. Three one-second tasks gathered like this finish in about one second total, not three.

display.code:
import asyncio
import time

async def task(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    print(f"{name} done")
    return name


async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(task("A", 1), task("B", 1), task("C", 1))
    print(f"concurrent: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")   # ~1s -- they ran together
    print(results)


asyncio.run(main())

beats.narration: asyncio.create_task gives you more control than gather -- the coroutine starts running in the background immediately, and you decide when, or even whether, to await its result. Here, both workers start right away, and only the awaits at the end actually block.

display.code:
import asyncio

async def worker(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    return n * n


async def main():
    task1 = asyncio.create_task(worker(2))   # starts running now
    task2 = asyncio.create_task(worker(3))   # also starts running now

    print("tasks are running in the background...")
    result1 = await task1
    result2 = await task2
    print(result1, result2)


asyncio.run(main())

beats.narration: Real async code usually needs to cap how much runs at once, so you don't hammer a server with ten thousand simultaneous requests. A semaphore does that -- wrap each fetch in async-with-semaphore, set the limit to three, and only three coroutines are ever mid-flight at the same time.

display.code:
import asyncio
import random

async def fetch(session_id, semaphore):
    async with semaphore:                     # only N fetches run at once
        await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0.1, 0.3))
        return f"result-{session_id}"


async def main():
    semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(3)          # at most 3 concurrent
    tasks = [fetch(i, semaphore) for i in range(10)]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    print(results)


asyncio.run(main())

beats.narration: By default, gather cancels everything else the moment one coroutine raises. Passing return_exceptions equals True changes that -- you get every result back, successes and exceptions side by side, so one bad fetch doesn't sink the whole batch.

display.code:
import asyncio

async def might_fail(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    if n == 2:
        raise ValueError(f"failed on {n}")
    return n * 10


async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        might_fail(1), might_fail(2), might_fail(3),
        return_exceptions=True,
    )
    for r in results:
        if isinstance(r, Exception):
            print("error:", r)
        else:
            print("ok:", r)


asyncio.run(main())

beats.narration: Not every slow operation should be allowed to run forever. asyncio.wait_for wraps a coroutine with a hard deadline -- if it doesn't finish in time, a TimeoutError is raised, and you can catch it, clean up, and move on instead of hanging indefinitely.

display.code:
import asyncio

async def slow_operation():
    await asyncio.sleep(5)
    return "finished"


async def main():
    try:
        result = await asyncio.wait_for(slow_operation(), timeout=1)
        print(result)
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        print("operation timed out")


asyncio.run(main())

beats.narration: So when do you actually reach for asyncio over the other two? Managing thousands of concurrent network connections -- asyncio scales far better than threads. Just a handful of blocking calls into existing libraries -- plain threading is often simpler. And when you need to mix blocking code into an async program, you run it in a thread pool through loop.run_in_executor.

display.heading: asyncio vs. threading vs. multiprocessing
display.subheading: Thousands of connections -> asyncio  |  a few blocking calls -> threading  |  heavy compute -> multiprocessing

beats.narration: Gather and semaphores get real concurrency out of a single thread. But notice what's missing -- nothing here guarantees a task you create actually gets checked on. That gap is exactly what structured concurrency closes.

display.heading: Concurrency without a guarantee -- yet
display.subheading: Next up: making sure every task is actually accounted for

beats.narration: Level four asyncio is about making concurrent code trustworthy in production -- guaranteeing that every task you start is actually accounted for, cleaned up, and its failures surfaced, instead of silently lost.

Fire-and-forget tasks are a real hazard. Call create_task and never await it, and if that coroutine raises, the exception can vanish -- swallowed, or reported late to stderr as 'task exception was never retrieved,' long after anyone could act on it.

display.code:
import asyncio

async def background_job():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    raise ValueError("something went wrong")


async def main():
    asyncio.create_task(background_job())   # fire-and-forget -- dangerous!
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    print("main finished")


asyncio.run(main())
# main finished
# (the ValueError inside background_job is silently swallowed -- or reported late, to stderr, as "Task exception was never retrieved")

beats.narration: Python 3.11's asyncio.TaskGroup fixes that structurally. Every task started inside the group is guaranteed to be awaited -- if one fails, the group automatically cancels its siblings and re-raises everything together as an ExceptionGroup, which you catch with the new except-star syntax.

display.code:
import asyncio

async def worker(name, delay, fail=False):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    if fail:
        raise ValueError(f"{name} failed")
    return f"{name} done"


async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(worker("A", 0.5))
            tg.create_task(worker("B", 0.3))
            tg.create_task(worker("C", 0.2, fail=True))
        print("all tasks succeeded")
    except* ValueError as eg:
        # except* is Python 3.11+ syntax for handling ExceptionGroups
        for exc in eg.exceptions:
            print(f"caught: {exc}")


asyncio.run(main())

beats.narration: Tasks can also be cancelled explicitly. A well-behaved coroutine catches CancelledError, does its cleanup, and then re-raises it -- swallowing it silently would trick whatever cancelled the task into thinking it's still running.

display.code:
import asyncio

async def long_running():
    try:
        print("starting long work")
        await asyncio.sleep(10)
        print("this line never runs if cancelled")
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("cleaning up after cancellation")
        raise   # convention: re-raise CancelledError after cleanup


async def main():
    task = asyncio.create_task(long_running())
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    task.cancel()
    try:
        await task
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("confirmed: task was cancelled")


asyncio.run(main())
display.output:
starting long work
cleaning up after cancellation
confirmed: task was cancelled

beats.narration: That semaphore pattern combines directly with TaskGroup. Here, twenty fake page fetches are bounded to five running at once, all launched inside a TaskGroup -- so you get both the concurrency cap and the guarantee that every task is awaited before the group exits.

display.code:
import asyncio

async def fetch_page(page_id, semaphore):
    async with semaphore:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.2)   # simulated I/O
        return f"page-{page_id}"


async def main():
    semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(5)   # at most 5 concurrent "fetches"
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(fetch_page(i, semaphore)) for i in range(20)]

    results = [t.result() for t in tasks]
    print(len(results), "pages fetched")


asyncio.run(main())

beats.narration: asyncio.timeout is a context-manager version of wait_for, and it composes naturally with TaskGroup -- wrap a whole group of tasks in a timeout block, and if it expires, every task in that group gets cancelled together, cleanly.

display.code:
import asyncio

async def slow_operation():
    await asyncio.sleep(5)
    return "done"


async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(1):
            result = await slow_operation()
            print(result)
    except TimeoutError:
        print("operation timed out and was cancelled cleanly")


asyncio.run(main())
display.output: operation timed out and was cancelled cleanly

beats.narration: For producer-consumer patterns, asyncio.Queue coordinates safely between coroutines, including backpressure through maxsize. A producer puts items on the queue, a consumer awaits queue.get in a loop, and a sentinel value like None signals there's nothing left to process.

display.code:
import asyncio

async def producer(queue, count):
    for i in range(count):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        await queue.put(i)
        print(f"produced {i}")
    await queue.put(None)   # sentinel value signaling "no more items"


async def consumer(queue):
    while True:
        item = await queue.get()
        if item is None:
            break
        print(f"consumed {item}")
        queue.task_done()


async def main():
    queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=5)
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tg.create_task(producer(queue, 5))
        tg.create_task(consumer(queue))


asyncio.run(main())

beats.narration: As a quick reference: TaskGroup runs tasks with guaranteed cleanup and propagation, except-star handles the ExceptionGroup it raises, task.cancel requests cancellation directly, asyncio.timeout cancels a whole block if it runs too long, Queue coordinates producers and consumers, and Semaphore caps how many coroutines run at once.

display.heading: Advanced asyncio cheat sheet
display.subheading: TaskGroup for cleanup  |  except* for ExceptionGroups  |  timeout, Queue, Semaphore for control

beats.narration: That's structured concurrency -- every task awaited, every failure surfaced, every timeout and cancellation handled cleanly. Put together with threading and asyncio's basics, that's the full concurrency toolkit Python gives you.
